title: HConvGLU for Channel Mixing in Image Encoders
summary: The forward pass of Mirage's channel mixer. Fixed Walsh transforms, three learned bands and a GELU gate, with the indexing, arithmetic and implementation details.
body_markdown:
Mirage's image encoder uses 512 channels to describe each cell of a 16×1616 \\times 16


16


×


16


image grid. Mixing those channels with a conventional feed-forward layer of hidden width 2048 would require about 2.1 million weights per block. Repeating that across the encoder would spend much of the model's storage on channel mixing alone.


HConvGLU uses a fixed Walsh transform to put each feature vector into another basis, mixes nearby coefficients with learned bands, then transforms back. A GELU gate makes the result depend nonlinearly on the input. The released encoder uses 28 of these mixers, each with 100,352 parameters. This article derives the forward pass, explains the restriction imposed by the bands and counts the work the operator actually performs.

A channel mixer operates within one feature vector. Spatial convolutions and attention move information between image locations. Keeping those jobs separate lets us ask a narrower question about the channel map. How much freedom do we need to give every pair of channels, and how much can a fixed transform supply?


The[Hadamard MLP](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/hadamard-mlp) in Needle learns structured Kronecker mixing factors. HConvGLU keeps the basis fixed and spends its learned parameters on bands inside that basis. The two constructions share a connection to Walsh-Hadamard transforms, but they define different families of functions.


[Gabor initialisation](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/gabor-initialisation) supplies a separate spatial bias to the encoder's convolutions. It changes their starting weights. HConvGLU defines the channel operator used throughout inference.

## Computing the transform


A dense matrix multiplication is unnecessary for WW


W


. The following NumPy implementation uses the same sequency butterfly as Mirage. It accepts any leading batch dimensions and transforms the last axis.


```text
import   numpy   as   np


def   walsh_sequency  (x):
x   =   np.array(x,   copy  =  True  )
n   =   x.shape[  -  1  ]
if   n   <   1   or   n   &   (n   -   1  ):
raise   ValueError  (  "the last dimension must be a power of two"  )
width   =   1
while   width   <   n:
blocks   =   x.reshape(  *  x.shape[:  -  1  ], n   //   (  2   *   width),   2  , width)
left   =   blocks[  ...  ,   0  , :]
signs   =   np.where(np.arange(width)   %   2   ==   0  ,   1  ,   -  1  )
right   =   blocks[  ...  ,   1  , :]   *   signs
x   =   np.stack((left   +   right, left   -   right),   axis  =-  1  ).reshape(x.shape)
width   *=   2
return   x   /   np.sqrt(n)
```

Against the specified dense baseline, HConvGLU stores about 20.9 times fewer parameters and uses about 21.7 times fewer band multiply-accumulates. Across 28 mixers the stored parameter counts are 2,809,856 versus 58,720,256. Neither ratio is an end-to-end latency ratio or an accuracy comparison. Memory access, transforms, activation functions and hardware utilisation determine the actual runtime.


## Where it sits in Mirage


Five stride-two stem stages reduce the 512-pixel canvas to a 16×1616 \\times 16


16


×


16


grid. The encoder then has 16 convolutional body blocks and 12 attention blocks. Each contains one HConvGLU at width 512.


In a body block, a gated depthwise convolution first mixes neighbouring spatial cells. A normalised feature vector enters HConvGLU, and global response normalisation acts on its output before the residual addition. The attention blocks instead follow their attention residual with normalisation, HConvGLU and a residual addition, without that response-normalisation wrapper. Valid-image masks keep padded cells out of the feature computation.


HConvGLU itself works on one feature vector at a time. Attention, spatial convolutions and the surrounding response normalisation supply the interactions between locations. Four register tokens participate in the attention stack and are removed from the image grid before the downstream heads use it. The[Mirage architecture diagram and maths](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage#inside-the-model) show these surrounding operations in full.

The bias is not rescaled. This equals the normalised expression above. A port using normalised butterflies should use the original bands, while one using the folded weights should use the unnormalised butterfly. Applying both scales would change the operator.


HConvGLU limits the learned channel map to make the encoder smaller.[Structured visuo-semantic perception](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/structured-perception) imposes structure at another level, by reducing the language decoder's responsibilities. Both choices are explicit restrictions on the model. Their practical value is whether the resulting model performs the required perception tasks within the device's storage and compute budget. The[Mirage release](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage) puts the complete system and its outputs in context.
